# GitHub merge queue: how it works and what happens on a conflict

How GitHub’s merge queue orders and tests pull requests, how to enable it, what happens when a queued pull request conflicts, and the alternatives.

Merget team · Nov 13, 2026 · 4 min read

GitHub’s merge queue lines up approved pull requests, tests each one together with the changes ahead of it, and merges it when the required checks pass. If a queued pull request conflicts with the base branch or fails a required check, GitHub removes it from the queue, and the author fixes it and queues again.

## What a merge queue is for

On a busy branch, a pull request can pass its checks and still break main, because it was tested against an older main. A merge queue closes that gap. It builds a temporary branch containing the target branch, the pull requests ahead in the queue and yours, runs your required checks on that combination, and merges only if they pass.

## How to enable merge queue on GitHub

  1. In the repository settings, edit the branch protection rule or ruleset for the target branch.
  2. Turn on Require merge queue, then choose the merge method and group settings.
  3. Update CI to run on the `merge_group` event, so required checks report on the queue’s temporary branches.
  4. On an approved pull request, select Merge when ready to add it to the queue.
    
    `on:
      pull_request:
      merge_group:`

GitHub documents which plans and repository types include merge queue, so check that before you plan around it. See managing a merge queue.

## How the queue groups and tests pull requests

The queue works in merge groups. Each group is a temporary branch, named with the `gh-readonly-queue/` prefix, that holds the target branch plus one or more queued pull requests in order. Your required checks run against that branch through the `merge_group` event.

jina.title: GitHub merge queue: how it works and what happens on a conflict
jina.snippet:
GitHub’s merge queue lines up approved pull requests, tests each one together with the changes ahead of it, and merges it when the required checks pass. If a queued pull request conflicts with the base branch or fails a required check, GitHub removes it from the queue, and the author fixes it and queues again.

## What a merge queue is for

On a busy branch, a pull request can pass its checks and still break main, because it was tested against an older main. A merge queue closes that gap. It builds a temporary branch containing the target branch, the pull requests ahead in the queue and yours, runs your required checks on that combination, and merges only if they pass.

3.   Update CI to run on the `merge_group` event, so required checks report on the queue’s temporary branches.
4.   On an approved pull request, select Merge when ready to add it to the queue.

```
on:
  pull_request:
  merge_group:
```

Without one, every landing triggers a round of rebases, and each rebase is another agent session and another CI run. With one, the sessions stop when their pull request is open. How GitHub’s merge queue orders and tests pull requests, how to enable it, what happens when a queued pull request conflicts, and the alternatives.

GitHub’s merge queue lines up approved pull requests, tests each one together with the changes ahead of it, and merges it when the required checks pass. If a queued pull request conflicts with the base branch or fails a required check, GitHub removes it from the queue, and the author fixes it and queues again.

What a merge queue is for

On a busy branch, a pull request can pass its checks and still break main, because it was tested against an older main. A merge queue closes that gap. parallel-fast.snippet:
How Merget’s semantic merge queue works.

Merget finds the pull requests that conflict, resolves them in queue order, and lands the result through your required checks and reviews.
Sign up free Book a call

Find conflicts Git can’t see.

A renamed function and a new call to its old name can merge cleanly and still break main. That is a semantic conflict: a conflict in meaning, not text.

Signature drift

Blocking A changed signature. A required parameter is added while a new caller elsewhere still passes the old arguments.
PR A, billing.ts: function charge(total, currency) PR B, checkout.ts: charge(order.total) Result: currency argument missing

Broken reference

Blocking A renamed helper leaves a caller behind. A helper is renamed on one branch while another branch adds a call to its old name.
PR A, format.ts: formatAmount → formatMoney PR B, invoice.ts: formatAmount(total) Result: formatAmount is no longer defined

Deleted dependency

Blocking A removed definition is still called. One change removes a definition that a different change still calls.
PR A, tax.ts: - function legacyTax(cart) PR B, checkout.ts: legacyTax(cart) Result: call to a removed definition

Duplicate definition

Review Two additions, one name. Two separate additions create the same fully qualified name. Ambiguous cases go to review.
PR A, retry.ts: export const RETRY_LIMIT = 3 PR B, retry.ts: export const RETRY_LIMIT = 5 Result: RETRY_LIMIT defined twice

Data flow

Advisory A changed policy reaches another reader. A changed policy value alters what another change reads.
PR A, policy.ts: maxRetries = 0 PR B, sync.ts: for (i < policy.maxRetries) retry() Result: sync now never retries

Confluence

Advisory Two edits feed one total. Independent edits, such as one to a price and one to a fee, feed into the same total.
PR A, price.ts: price = base * 1.10 PR B, fees.ts: serviceFee = 4.00 Result: both change order.total

Override

Advisory A value replaced before it is used. Writes on interacting path

Run your normal required checks on the pull request, then send it through a merge queue so it is tested against the main it will actually land on. Batching keeps that affordable at high volume, and Prevention flags new flaky tests before they merge.

By Julien Danjou, Co-founder & CEO of MergifyUpdated November 4, 2026

## In one paragraph

An AI-generated pull request fails the same way a human one does, so it gets the same required checks. What changes is how many are open at once. Each one was tested against a main that has moved by the time it merges, and two green changes can break main together. A merge queue closes that gap: it builds each pull request on the latest main and everything ahead of it, runs your CI on that exact state, and merges only if it passes. Batching stops this from costing one full pipeline per pull request, and Prevention reruns new tests so the flaky ones get flagged while the pull request is still open.

The traffic. A type error or a failing test looks the same whoever typed the code, so the checks can stay as they are. But an agent can open a dozen pull requests in the time a person opens one, work overnight, and touch the same files as another agent running next to it.
